Jurassic World: Evolution is a game that is stilted, sterile and constrictive in its park building gameplay, level design and soundtrack. Being a spiritual successor to 2003’s Jurassic Park: Operation Genesis, it somehow manages to come short of doing certain things better than its predecessor even with the impressive and amazing visuals, increased dinosaur roster and DLCs.

Its park building management is incredibly shallow and the game feels largely incomplete despite the current dinosaur roster size and especially without the DLC packs. 

I cannot recommend the base game of Jurassic World: Evolution because you’d be starved for building content and the extra animals. You NEED to get all the DLCs to make Jurassic World: Evolution to feel like a “complete” package which the game is not despite the game’s finished post-launch development. Even then you need to install mods to help resolve certain issues that Frontier didn’t even bother with.

[hr][/hr] 
As previously mentioned, Jurassic World: Evolution’s dinosaur models are astounding to look at but the gameplay leaves much to be desired and it often feels like the game is fighting back against you. From the annoying terrain constraints when placing buildings, the non-streamlined minimal designed user interface that requires to redundantly click additional menus to get anywhere and a seemingly lack of shortcut keys for getting into the paths and buildings menu.

Terrain tools are the absolute laziest bare minimum to edit an island. Every island is walled in and restrictive and there isn’t even an island generator for sandbox. Decorations used to be non-existent until late into the game’s lifespan when players were constantly requesting it for months. There really isn’t any way to personalize your park more with a simple water fountain, benches, trash cans or dinosaur skeletons for display. And this is coming from the same people who made Planet Coaster and later, Planet Zoo.

Gone are the weather calendar forecasts from JPOG, where you’re able to prep and be ready for the upcoming tornados. Now storm protection buildings only give a miss-able notification on the top right of your screen mere minutes before an actual damaging storm or tornado to come pushing through.

Contracts from the three divisions; science, entertainment and security may seem like a good idea in concept, but holy hell, it’s probably one of the biggest annoying things in the game. Three ego maniacs that are suppose to be working together to ensure the park’s success can actively try to sabotage the safety of your park and guests, never mind actually getting your animals sick as well. Completely breaking my immersion of the game, I would’ve expected an outside party attempting to sabotage the park instead like BioSyn or some other new corporate rival. Not three criminals who get jealous and ruin my park because I didn’t do something for them, it’s borderline childish and insane for all three division characters to do this.

Guests have become a complete afterthought in comparison to Jurassic Park: Operation Genesis. They have utterly stripped the “humanity” of their guests. No character, personality or charm. They neither use umbrellas when it rains or storms, nor do they hold or use Jurassic World/Park merchandise when they purchase something from the gift shop. Frontier couldn’t even be bothered to add a mechanic regarding what guests like/dislike; such as thrill seekers watching carnivores fight for example.

There’s also a strange lack of attractions in comparison to what was seen in the film(s). No petting zoo, flying-fox ziplines, water slides or even the water cruise. There aren’t even sea reptiles or most of the flying reptiles* shown in the first Jurassic World movie. All missing and were never added via a DLC before the announcement of the sequel. If you wanted to build and customize your own lagoon and aviary like in the film, tough luck, you’ll have to wait three years for Jurassic World: Evolution 2 to give you that.

This is why I said Jurassic World: Evolution feels largely incomplete, there’s a lot of content that you would naturally expect to be included, but wasn’t. Even the sequel game has its own issues despite the limited improvements it advertises.

[hr][/hr]
Dinosaur behaviour was, and somehow still is, abysmal. Frontier had to gradually update the dinosaurs to do something as simple as sleeping and herding post-launch and there's still no pack hunting. Disappointing lack of dynamic dinosaur behaviour and unique fight/kill animations (with a small handful of exceptions), including dinosaurs breaking out. Velociraptors don’t climb fences anymore and every animal in the game simply bashes its skull against any type of fence, which themselves are incredibly weak.

The way the dinosaur mechanics are handled is irritating to say the least. Dinosaur comfort can actively decrease while there’s raining weather. Velociraptors are infamous for getting head trauma, knocking down fences and escaping, thus whenever wet weather arrives, I immediately have to send out a jeep or helicopter to tranquilize my carnivores because they’re so fragile.

[hr][/hr]
The game is also not entirely well optimized in terms of performance. Running the game on a Ryzen 5 3600 and GTX 1070, it can still chug at times, especially with the increased guest population as your park grows with increased number of dinosaurs and ratings.

Accessing the expedition dig site menu can sometimes dip the framerate below 60FPS for some unknown reason. Moving around in it, I can see and feel the menu camera stutter slightly with its frame-pacing. It’s incredibly bizarre for the game to do that.

Guest numbers can tank your framerate as well and there’s no option (unlike in Planet Zoo) to help decrease the number of in-game human models being loaded and walking around in your park. Apparently, this is a huge issue with Frontier’s use of the Cobra engine from Planet Coaster, Planet Zoo and their Jurassic World: Evolution franchise. 

It is concerning that such optimization issues still persist throughout their games. The only way to get decent framerate stability is to brute force the game with more powerful hardware, which isn’t exactly worth the investment for a single game or if you’re already hard on cash.

[hr][/hr]
Frontier makes a lot of “raised eyebrows” decisions, issues that could’ve been easily addressed during development before launch that didn’t require constant player and fan feedback to be shot at the developers for them to attempt to fix and update most of the issues months later. There are elements and things to like and even love about Jurassic World: Evolution, but they’ll always be overshadowed by Frontier’s tedious, frustrating and restrictive game design.

I cannot recommend Jurassic World: Evolution and all its DLCs at full price. Get this game on sale and install mods to tackle some of the issues that Frontier has obviously failed to address before they moved on to their sequel. Having pre-ordered this game back in 2018, did I have fun? Yeah, sure I did but I had to actively find it before staying away from the game for two years or so then coming back and using mods to alienate some of the dissatisfaction I had.

A remarkably shallow game.  Someone else said this, I'm just agreeing with them.

Let me give you an example:  There are a lot of dinosaurs in the game, which is cool at first, but every single dinosaur acts the same.  All the meat eaters act the same as all the other meat eaters, no matter if it's a T-Rex or a Dilophosaurus.  All the plant eaters act the same as all the rest.  The difference is that every single Dino has their own "welfare" stat screen, and every single dino likes different things.  For example, a T-Rex likes a BIG paddock, and a Maiasaurus likes having other Maia's with them (3+).  But if you change these things then the Dino's "Comfort" stat drops into the red, and every single Dinosaur, INCLUDING the carnivores and herbivores, act the same exact way.  They go for the fence and try to break through.  NOTHING ELSE.

Another example:  I created a pack of velociraptors thinking that I was really doing myself in.  That I was going to have fun managing these mischievous little things.  But once I got the pack into their comfort zone, nothing ever happened.  They stayed in their pen, they ran around.  People looked at them.  NOTHING.  They didn't coordinate a breakout.  They didn't wreak havoc on me.  They were just Generic Dinosaur #15.

And like I said, while it is cool at first that there's 30+ dino's, the maps are so small / the scaling is so off that you'll never ever ever have more than 10 or 15 dino type's in your entire park.  On one map I spent hours filling the entire thing to the brim with nothing but paddocks, buildings, paths, and no free space.  I literally had paddocks surrounding the entrance path into the main "village" of the park.  And that gave me 14 separate types of dinosaurs.  If I introduced 1 more dinosaur, either by number or by type, it would have caused the entire pack to become "unhappy."

While at first it seems like there's a lot of content like building types, you realize that you're just mistaking the **slow** drip of content that you can use through the campaign as depth.

Worst, though, is that you'd think these trade offs of shallow maps, shallow dinosaurs, shallow design, shallow gameplay would have given us good graphics.  But the graphics are mediocre at best.


Ultimately it's worth it as a time killer if you can pick it up on sale.  But not at full price.

Now that that's out of the way, I'd like to share my personal opinions of JWE as both it's own game and as a spiritual successor to Jurassic park: Operation Genesis. I have seen COUNTLESS people on steam comparing JWE to JPOG as measure of the new game's overall quality. There is nothing inherently wrong with this, as most of us are fully aware that Frontier took heavy inspiration from JPOG while developing their new title. The problem arises when people allow their childhood memories to ruin their present objectivity. "JPOG was so much better" "this game is so disappointing compared to jpog" "jpog was part of my childhood! This game just pales in comparison". 

If you've said anything along these lines when voicing your opinion on Jurassic world Evolution, I have an important message for you: Rose tinted amnesia goggles are a dangerous trap. As somebody who still has a functioning ps2 copy of JPOG that they played up until the release of JWE, i can tell you that JWE is superior to JPOG in almost every way. 
---over twice the dinosaurs
---more animation diversity and quality(no more awkward walk pivoting that was presnt in jpog)
---greater sound diversity and quality. The sound is seriously incredible in this game. So many variations on classic movie sounds thrown in with unique grunts, growls and bellows that really make the dinos feel like they actually have working lungs and vocal resonation chambers instead of just being robots that repeat the same 2 roar sound effects over and over again. (jpog t rex *cough*) 
---POWER MANAGEMENT (brings new factors and hazards into maintaing a park which is a great addition. All of Jpog's buildings, fences ect ran magically with no need for electricity. 

---greater ways to get close and interact with dinosaurs. I.E. ranger jeep, pictures, acu helicopter tranqulizing, drivable gyro spheres ect. 
---better enclosure building tools: rounded fence shaping, abiltiy to REPLACE existing fence pieces instead of rebuilding from scratch, and you can actually build enclosures close to and even on top of each other. In jpog every habitat was a giant square/rectangle that had to be at least a couple units away from the other habitats. 

---Lots a great little details; favorite examples include: Idominus Rex has a unique eating animation. It can also share an enclosure with Velociraptors. Which makes sense given it shares half of it's DNA with raptors. I also enjoy wathcing the dinosaurs approach inqusitively, become angry or flee in terror from the ranger jeep. I have heard people complain that the dinosaurs should be able to wreck your jeep or kill your rangers. This is a neat idea in paper, but i guarantee that if you have a park with 100 creatures in it, and you're trying to manage guest happiness, send out expeditions, extract DNA from fossils and prevent a rabies outbreak simultaneously, you're going to get real sick of that trike destroying your jeep every time you drive it into the enclosure to heal it of it's disease. 

******WAY more customization options for Dinos themselves like colors, gene splicing, names ect. 
you couldnt even name dinos in jpog. if you had 8 T-rexes, they were all green with black stripes and were called "Tyrannosaurus-Rex". How exciting. 

---Very intuitive UI that is easy to navigate  and allows you to locate specific dinosaurs and structures throughout the park easily. 

---Has an UNLIMITED number of dinosaurs that can exist on an island. Far exceeding JPOG's 60 dinosaur limit. 

 Most the guest needs that were present in jpog are mirrored in JWE, the main difference being that they are seen through the facility rating menu instead of clicking on each tiny guest model to see what they specifically want to see in your park (like in jpog). I would like to see a bit more guest interation myself as that does give more meaning to all the amenities you build in the park instead of just looking at numbers go up in a menu. It is a lot more fun in my opinion to watch guest get killed in JWE though lol. 


While it is true that jpog had a FEW more item placement options like garabage cans, fountians benches ect, it's also a shame that those things are ultimately inconsequential and uninteresting. You see a guest complain that he's tired, you throw down some benches (that are so tiny you can barely see them) and you never bother with them again. Doesn't add much to the game in my opinion. 

One of my favorite things about JWE is the fact that it actually has a lot of content. Especially when compared to JPOG. Plentiful amounts of optional contracts and objectives that not only contribute to reputation amoung the game's 3 factions, but allow you to unlock additonal buildings, dinosaurs, skin colors and more. I was very pleased that I actually had to earn that five star rating in each island. It was a delicate balancing act that would would rise and fall naturally as I progressed through the building process of my park. The point is, it was a fun journey that took time and effort. The Progression was satisfying. So far I've been able to acheive a 5 star rating on all of the islands except Isla Sorna. Im about 30 hours in. In JPOG, in my most recent playthrough, I was able to 5 star my park in less than two hours. TWO hours. And that's the main meat and potatoes of the entire game. 

******complaints******
Please note that there ARE caveats to Jurassic World Evolution. There is The occasional small bug, and Animation variety in combat specifically could use some expansion. The guest interaction is also somewhat limited as i mentioned earlier. (although this doesn't bother me personally as much because the dinosaurs are the star of the show anyway). It also would be nice to see the dinosaurs be able to sleep naturally. 

TL;DR: Jurassic World evolution is fun, beautiful and well worth 60$. Despite leaving a little to be desired in some areas like animation variety, building space and guest interactivity, the game far exceeds Operation genesis as the definitive dinosaur park builder game. Frontier has created an amazing expereince with this game and i can't wait to see what content they release down the road. If you loved JPOG, you will love this game too. 

******Last note to people comparing this game to Operation Genesis*******

It's perfectly fine if you personally think JWE is flawed and ultimately not worth your money. It is flawed, but it's also well designed and has a great deal to offer to both dinosaur and park builder enthusiasts. If you feel the need to voice your opinions, try to remain objective and avoid clouding your judgement by wearing the biased goggles of fond memories. There seems to be a great deal of people that are band wagoning negativity for this game and spewing into an echo chamber hoping to validate their feelings of disappointment that they ultimately created for themselves by failing to manage their expectations and using childhood memories as a foundation on which to base their critique. To me, it not only makes for a weak argument but also completely dismisses the merits that JWE has as a game on it's own. Which could cause people to avoid it for the wrong reasons.  Don't be one of those people that play like 8-15 hours of this game (half of that spent alt-tabbed), then immediately jump into this text box and start complaining that the game feels unfinished when they have yet to experience  70% of the game's unlocks or content. It's only natural that a game will feel unfinished if you haven't finished it yet. Who knew?

First, the good: the dinosaurs are, as others have said, superbly well-done. Well-designed and well-animated, they really are a joy to just sit and watch. 

It's pity then that the game that surrounds them is an otherwise joyless experience. The building is clunky: it's difficult to make paths and enclosures follow the terrain, and building placement is a bit finicky. Neat rows of buildings or paths that follow parallel to enclosures take an inordinate amount of effort. The selection of buildings is pretty anemic, and there's little in the way of customization, so you'll see the same exact sort of building repeated quite a bit. The 'decor' is laughable: half a dozen boulders and a small selection of scrawny trees. There's absolutely no artificial decor: no fountains, or flowerbeds, or trashcans or streetlights. So simply as a park designer, the game fails through a lack of items and building tools. 

Perhaps this might be forgiven if the management side of things was engaging but, alas, it's even more of a hot mess. Getting a stable cash flow is all but guaranteed: half a dozen dinosaurs will net you at least 100k in ticket sales every minute (even if you hilariously have just a couple hundred guests). Your real job as manager is to perform 'contracts' for three Ingen divisions, Entertainment, Science, and Security. Doing these earns you favor, which leads to rewards in the form of new buildings and dinos. The missions are randomly generated from the same basic pool (all three divisions, for example, ask you to release new dinos, or build new structures). There's no flavor or difference: just grind out random quests like in a sub-par MMO. And because doing a contract for 1 division lowers your 'rep' with the other two, getting all the rewards means grinding for an exceedingly long time on every scenario.  This, no doubt, was the point of the system. 

If you didn't buy your management sim to go questing, you can always attempt to do a bit of research and development, a task which is in no way linked to the science division (which is more interested in paying you 100 grand to get a dilo and raptor to fight than it is in doing science). Actual research advancement requires you to spend an unfortunate amount of time paging through various UI screens. All the component activities, fossil hunting, DNA extraction, research, are on timers, so every couple minutes you have to stop what you are dong and go check on them. It starts off feeling like a mobile game, but quickly descends into being a chore. At no point does it really approach being fun. 

In terms of actually managing your park, there's very little to do. You can make a few superficial choices of the sort that Hammond probably let his grandkids decide (should the giftshop sell hats or shirts?). No setting ticket prices (or hotel prices) and no creating zones and charging extra admission. There are no restrooms (guests apparently just go in the bushes like the dinos), and no trash system. You hire rangers in Jeeps and rangers in helicopters, but no janitors, scientists, or even guys in dino suits. 

One can go on for some time about the lesser problems. About how all guest needs (fun, food, shopping) are meant exclusively through buildings, so that a bowling alley, fast food joint, and clothing store do far more to raise guest satisfaction than a Trike exhibit. Apparently my guests are paying $3000 dollars a minute for the experience of a Midwestern strip mall. Or about questionable UI decisions, like the notification for a diseased dinosaur that, when clicked, takes you to a map which you then have to exit out of to go summon the ranger to medicate the dino. The short answer is that despite the gorgeous dinosaurs, the game works neither as a casual park builder nor as a deep management sim. I got this game for 80% off ($9) and I still think I overpaid.

[h1]Jurassic World Evolution Review[/h1]
Jurassic World Evolution is a business simulation game that allows players to build a dinosaur theme park and was developed and published by Frontier Developments. It is based on the 2015 film “Jurassic World” and the game was released on June 2018 for PC, PS 4 and Xbox. A much similar game to this one is Planet Zoo. They are the same genre but JWE (Jurassic World Evolution) has dinosaurs instead of animals. The game has a career mode in which you need to develop five-stars parks across the fictional islands of the Las Cinco Muertes Archipelago and features more than 40 types of dinosaurs. Also, their genes can be modified to introduce new features.

[h1]What makes this game unique[/h1]
This game has some unique features. One of them is the ability to bring dinosaurs to life. As the game says, “dinosaurs will feel and react intelligently to the world you build around them”. Another interesting feature is that you can choose your own path. By that, I mean that you can build for science, entertainment or security interests. At last, the feature that I fancy the most is that if a player’s reputation within a division gets too low, a sabotage will be created. For example: the park’s power will be shut down and the dinosaurs will be able to break out. Another example is that a disease could be introduced to infect them.
The dinosaurs are controlled by artificial intelligence and will interact with each other and the environment. For example, Carnivores will attack Carnivores of a different species and they will hunt Herbivores.
Also, there is a sandbox mode. The sandbox mode is unlocked once a four-star park rating is achieved on the starting island and is set on Isla Nublar, the setting of the movie. Once this is achieved, everything a player has unlocked in career mode will be available in the sandbox mode (building upgrades and dinosaurs). If the player hasn’t unlocked something in career mode, that something won’t be available in the sandbox.

[h1]Art design[/h1]
The graphics for this game are stunning. The shadowing in combination with the lighting is perfect and the details are amazing. The dinosaurs are very detailed and look very good. They almost look real. And with the help of the photo mode, you can go drive a car along the island to see the lovely dinosaurs in their habitat. Also, I think that the animations of the dinosaurs look very convincing, immersing you into the game.

[h1]Is it still worth it?[/h1]
The game is one of the few dinosaur games out there. So, if you love the Jurassic Park movies or you are a dinosaur fanatic or you just simply like business simulation games, I can surely say this game is for you. And with the addition of the Return to Jurassic Park DLC, I can say that this game is still worth it. The DLC includes park features and locations form the original Jurassic Park film (the first one). The DLC also includes the island Isla Sorna which was featured in two of the Jurassic Park movies.
I wouldn’t recommend it for full price, as it offers a lot of quality game time that doesn’t get repetitive as you play, because of all the new features and achievements that you can unlock.

Can be challenging but not too hard.

Not encountered many bugs (yet!).

Dinosaurs seem to die of old age fairly quickly. - Maybe in the future the devs should allow the players to toggle the age settings for the dinos.

Dinosaur fighting is kind of lame. - The animations are VERY limited and don't even sync up properly for most fights. THIS NEEDS TO CHANGE as it ruins the immersion and also makes it seem kind of cheap. I'd love to see a proper battle between two of the carnivores rather than them standing and biting eachother in turns for a few minutes, resulting in the same old finishing move at the end. I think the fights also need to be more 'random' in how they pan out, for example, the raptor will always beat the Deinonychus every time, even though they should be a good match, which is boring. It would also be good to see more than just 1v1s, for example a group of Raptors trying to take down a T-rex would be so much better!

Human deaths. - Humans die when dinosaurs knock them over, which is kind of strange. Fair enough if they are trampled by a huge herbivore, but they will die even if a raptor touches them. This is both odd and annoying as it damages your park rating. The animations when humans are eaten are ok but get old quickly. Humans will aways run, then the animation sequence kicks in meaning they will fall over and then be eaten - EVERY TIME.

Dinos are killing machines. - Carrying on from Human deaths, carnivores will kind of just keep killing and eating humans until they are stopped. I don't think this should happen unless they are starving or in some sort of hunting mindset.

Dinosaur AI. - Sometimes it's a bit weird. E.g. they will be happy about the amount of grass in their enclosure but angry about the lack of trees, then they walk to the other side of their cage where the trees are and then be happy about the amount of trees but angry about the lack of grass. This often leads to them wanting to break out of the fence, even though their enclosure has everthing they want. Another feature that needs to be added could be individual dino personalities, i.e. traits outside of their genetic properties. For example, some might be angrier than others because at the moment they all act the same.

Dinosaur interaction. - There needs to be more communication between groups of the same species and pack hunting for the Raptors and stuff. When Raptors break out they just split up immediately and seek out prey and fights individually, which is the complete opposite to the movies.

Your income is so high that you can afford everything and nothing really goes wrong unless there is a breakout or a storm. The maps are fairly small, have annoying terrain and have frustrating jagged boundaries.

No mods or workshop yet.

This is kind of a two part review for Jurassic World Evolution & Return to Jurassic Park. Pretty straightforward game & DLC to review if I'm honest, it's excellent.

In terms of what it is that makes it so good, I think I'll leave the player to discover that by themselves. It really is something special and clearly a labour of love from the people behind it, the fan service is paramount here and really helps to invest the player in the 'Jurassic' experience. But here's a few of my personal favourites anyway:

Granted, I started playing this game on Playstation when it first hit shelves and have put far more hours into it on that than I did on Steam but to be completely fair and honest there is little to no difference between the two versions, albeit with improved framerates and resolution which is a-given with PC gaming anyway. I came back to this game after the Return to Jurassic Park DLC dropped, another great addition to the world adding in new designs and functions from the 1993 movie including the original appearances of the dinosaurs (with the far superior looking Rex, I did hate the Jurassic World look for her lol). I played the new campaign that it includes to completion and beyond, it really was worth the money at the time and still is now, especially if you're a die-hard fan of the original Spielberg series like myself.

I think the only major problem or annoyance that I personally had with this title was just the constant, and I mean constant moral slap across the wrist you have to repeatedly suffer through from Dr. Ian Malcolm regarding your decisions to introduce new species to the island network (which Evolution has a tremendous amount of, it's quite impressive). It can really start to grate on your nerves after about the 40th time, you start to feel as if you're a bad person and that you're doing something wrong, that you're going to be judged for it later on. Which, obviously in the 1993 film his role was to attempt to convince John Hammond that what he was doing was morally wrong and I suppose if it was really you in John's position you start to feel perhaps how he did eventually toward his vision for the park and obviously [spoiler]after Nedry's betrayal in Jurassic Park leading to the deaths of countless people and the release of the dinosaurs[/spoiler] trust between the staff is in very short supply. Yet, I can't help but feel that the idea behind the game is to give you the freedom to make those mistakes or attain those achievements freely, but in some way, as I mentioned, it feels like you're constantly being punished for.. just having fun I guess. This is way more apparent in Return to Jurassic Park where he plays a much bigger role in the alternative 'What-if' campaign scenario where the original movie cast return to voice their characters in a last ditch effort to save what is left of Jurassic Park and return it to it's former glory, almost every single piece of spoken dialogue is interrupted with 'Yes, but..' or 'Aren't you forgetting..?' it eventually came to a point where I was thinking to myself. 'No, we're moving on' because constantly bringing up the past is destroying the atmosphere, even while the rest of the cast such as Dr. Alan Grant & Ellie Sattler even John Hammond himself are very much onboard and genuinely trying to make a difference to save the dinosaurs and protect the public at the same time he still does very little to help in feeling like you're making any real progress.

Regardless, it's a minor gripe in a game that's simply a-wash with great content and visuals. The economic structure of income and expense can actually be fairly difficult to manage especially during times of emergency or visitor deaths but not impossible as there are many different sources of income, the idea behind sending expeditions to dig sites and discovering new viable DNA to create new species is good fun, behind able to modify their code at a genetic level to create new skin patterns and better stats for surviving or fighting adds a lot of depth to the core mechanics of the game itself. I find one of the best aspects of the Jurassic World campaign is that everybody is backing you, including fan-favourites like Chris Pratt's Owen Grady or Bryce Dallas Howard's Claire Dearing constantly pushing you into new realms of research, much like the mono-cur in the movie "Bigger, louder, more teeth." Making you feel like it really is best for business as the patrons of the park demand to see more and more variation of species, eventually forcing you into darker more inhumane realms such as creating the [spoiler]Indominus Rex[/spoiler] from the original Jurassic World or even the amazing [spoiler]Indoraptor[/spoiler] from the sequel Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom (Which they released a free species DLC pack in celebration of it's release adding in dinos from the movie). You're less of a humanitarian and become more of a self-proclaimed god especially if you play the Secrets of Dr. Wu DLC where you can start to create impossible species of your own design, strange hybrids and creatures that physically couldn't ever exist.

All in all there is a so much creative freedom here to discover, something that I haven't come across since my time playing Jurassic Park: Operation Genesis back in the early 2000's. I wholeheartedly recommend this to not only fans of the license but anybody that's interested in dinosaurs or even just park management simulations, I think there's something for everybody here and on sale or not it's worth every bit of time and money you put into it.

I waited a long time to buy Jurassic World Evolution because the reviews were always mixed to lower positive for this kind of game. I got it on sale because I worried I wouldn't like it. For reference, I love all the Jurassic Park movies (saw the first one in a packed theater, loved the second, and even loved the corniness of the third), but I did [i]not[/i] care for the recent Jurassic World movies. I also read the original novel of Jurassic Park when I was a little girl. I love dinosaurs, this IP, and simulation games.

I [i]really[/i] liked this game. It is not perfect, and it is much easier/simpler than I expected for a game of its kind. I do not own any DLC, so everything I talk about will be in the base game. It comes with 44 dinosaurs, many of which you unlock through fossil expeditions across a world map, a five-island campaign, challenges, and a sandbox mode. Unfortunately, sandbox does require you unlock everything through the campaign first (I tried playing sandbox after the first campaign island just to discover this). On each island, you will build exhibits, ensure they are an adequate environment for the types of dinosaurs, install herbivore/carnivore feeders, build guest buildings to meet their needs (food, drink, fun, shopping, etc.), and complete goal-related contracts for three divisions (science, entertainment, security). There are Operations buildings you need as well--Expedition Centers, Research Centers, ACU Center (helicopters for tranquilizing and transport for when dinos are getting naughty or you want to sell/move them), and Ranger center where Jeeps are kept with workers who drive around and medicate dinos, refill feeders, etc.

For the most part, all of this works flawlessly. The only glitch or hiccup I remember experiencing was the clip-through of a T-Rex head through her exhibit wall, but that was funny more than anything. One of the biggest negatives I have seen said about the game is the risk of sabotage by one of the divisions if you neglect them. See, the three aforementioned divisions all want you to do contracts and missions for them. When you do a contract for security, for example, your reputation with them goes up +2 and down -1 with the other two divisions. This makes contracts a game you have to play very carefully, because if your reputation with one of the divisions is too low, they might sabotage you (infecting a few dinosaurs with disease, cutting the power to a section of the park, etc.). I understand the choice of the developer to put this in there--after all, if you learn only one thing from the Jurassic Park books/movies, it's that people are backstabbing and greedy. But is it [i]annoying[/i]? Meh, a little. The sabotage methods are easily fixed. The only time I got annoyed with being sabotaged is when I was busy trying to do a million other things (capture escapees rampaging through the park, etc.). 

All screw-ups you make in-game are easily fixed, speaking of how easy this game is. If a dinosaur escapes and murders a bunch of people, your park rating will go down a little bit for a few minutes, and your guest count might drop 10% or so. But when money is overflowing from the coffers (which it will 95% of the time), it's just a matter of waiting it out until people conveniently forget that Aunt Martha gave Tinkletoes the T-Rex indigestion. If one division hates your guts because of low reputation, it's simply a matter of doing contracts for them until it's better (without neglecting the others). There is definitely room in the simulation genre for simulation games that offer challenge but are more often than not [i]relaxing[/i], and that is exactly what Jurassic World Evolution is. While many see this as a negative, I saw it as a breath of fresh air.

However, I did say the game isn't perfect. It is supremely vague when it comes to telling the player how to unlock things. You have to unlock pretty much everything: most dinosaur species, fossil dig sites, guest buildings, research items, even missions for island 2 and beyond. How do you do that? Hell if I know--and I've beaten the game. Most of the time, I just waited until new options came available. But I realized twenty hours in and on the last island that there are tons of things I didn't know and was never taught about how to unlock things. For example, all those Operations buildings I talked about earlier? You need to build AND keep them on all islands, or else it blocks you from unlocking certain research items and dig sites later on. I was selling all the unnecessary buildings once I'd exhausted dig sites or researched everything--because, well, I want to save space in my park, make a little money, and they were sitting there doing nothing anyway. Nope! I ended up having to travel back to each previous island I'd already beaten to rebuild them later, because it was keeping me from unlocking dinosaur breeds that were required for later main quests. You [i]can[/i] see some unlock requirements by going into the reputation menus--something I learned, again, twenty hours in by digging around. I basically ended up playing through the game twice because I missed so much the first time around and stunted my parks in the end. Thank goodness it was fun and the game saves your progress on previous islands, so it wasn't too much of an irritation to go back.

Like I said, I've beat the game and five-starred all islands. What's left? Mopping up some achievements. Will I ever return? Probably. This was a wonderful and relaxing simulation game that offers you many ways to experience Jurassic Park. You, yourself, can fly in helicopters and tranquilize dinosaurs, ride monorails or gyrospheres, and drive the ranger Jeeps in and out of exhibits. These are things I could only dream of in a simulation game back in the 90s. Having this game as a kid would've blown my mind. Could it have used expansion? Sure. While I think the dinosaur breeds encompass all the greats from the movies and even some obscure favorites, the exhibit environments could have used a little differentiation. You do unlock a lot of different "skins" for most dinos that visually differentiate them, and some of them are really cool. But all in all, I am really happy with this game and highly recommend it.

Okay, so after playing around 40 hours of the game, I guess I'll review it now. Note that I have not 100% completed the game (I still need to finish Isla Sorna), but I think I have seen enough to give an honest review in its current state.

Pros:
- Graphics - the game looks great, with bright, colourful environments, and awesome looking dinosaurs - at first glance the dinosaurs seem very real and like real animals wandering around their enclosure - but I'll talk more about that later.
- Unlockable Content - there's a fair amount of unlockable upgrades, buildings and dinosaurs through out the game, though I wish there were a few more things, primarily visitor buildings, at the end of the game e.g. rides like a rollercoaster.
- Divisions and Contracts - I liked this idea of having three divisions who are fighting for your attention, with different jobs they want you to do - but this system has some problems, I'll mention later.
- Fun - so far I've very much enjoyed my time playing the game - I guess due to the nostalgia, as I'm a huge Jurassic Park fan, and loved Jurassic Park: Operation Genesis/ JP:OG(probably my favourite game of all time)
- Sound Design - the sounds are really accurate to the Jurassic franchise (except some of Spinosaurus' roars lol), and the voice acting is good (Jeff Goldblum being the highlight), but Owen Grady (not played by Chris Pratt), falls flat in my opinion.

Cons:
- Limitations of Dinosaur Behaviour - after awhile the dinosaurs feel predictable - they wander, socialize, eat, drink and fight, and sometimes breakout and attack visitors... but they never sleep, herd or hunt in a pack. They do look very cool, but the repeated animations and behaviour starts to get boring - I'm happy to see Indoraptor has a lot of unique animations.
- Repetition of Contracts/Lack of Replayability - while I like the contracts system, you are often given almost the exact same one over and over, sometimes with the same dialouge from the characters. The missions also feel like there will be little replayability of them after I finish all of them - some of them are a bit annoying, while some I enjoyed the challenge
- Dinosaur Size Problems - for some reason, some of these are really inconsistent (with canon or real-life science), Spinosaurus and Giganotosaurus seem tiny to their real sizes (pathetic compared to the Rex), while others like Kentrosaurus, Styracosaurus and Tyrannosaurus seem a bit too large - and Ceratosaurus is gigantic, like what the hell lol
- Building/Terrain Controls - I found this finicky and annoying at times, though this might just be me. The terrain controls are pretty simple, but this may be a result of it being ported to console as well.

Summary (sort of):

I just think this game needs more content to be truly great, and the above issues need improvement. A randomised island where you have to get it to 5 stars, along with more missions linked to new islands could be cool. Other features from JP:OG could be included - e.g. dinosaurs sleeping, dinosaurs falling into comas, tornados being lethal, lethal force / other security measures against dinosaurs (turrets, rifle, aviodence beacon, lysine contigency etc.), and the one I want the most.... SITE B, like a proper one - dinosaurs can't properly live wild at the moment - herbivores rely on feeders, which need refilling.

Jurassic World Evolution is a difficult game to review conclusively, because it is both brilliant and terrible at what it does, almost in equal measure.  Overall, I've enjoyed playing the game despite some substantial problems, so I've given it a cautious 'recommended' rather than 'not recommended'...


[h1]The good stuff[/h1]

Right from the start, Jurassic World Evolution feels like a big-budget game.  It is a highly polished product with no bugs whatsoever, a gorgeously simple user interface and enough tutorial to start people on their way.  The graphics are richly detailed for the most part, and the sound and music is nothing short of stellar (right up there with blockbuster movies).  Every dinosaur comes with history and facts that are enjoyable to read in-game.  It exudes the atmosphere of Jurassic Park (the movie), the actors really voice their parts well and believably, and you feel central to that plot - with a mixture of wonder that you're even incubating dinosaur genomes, coupled with a sense of the madness and danger of it all.   The game works right from first install and feels like a finished experience rather than "a first shot at it" like many games feel nowadays.

What this game is NOT is another theme-park designer - and that is a mistake many buyers have made judging by the reviews.  This incorrect assumption is likely because this title is made by Frontier, who also brought us the highly design-creative Planet Coaster game.  However, Jurassic World Evolution is not about designing your own idea of a park so much as it is 'be in the movie'.  It's important to understand that before buying.  I've spent close to 50 hours in the game and haven't tired of it or run out of things to do just yet, but the fun is not in the designing itself, but in evolving dinosaurs and pushing the boundaries of your research as you try to make more thrilling, colourful and capable species to delight the crowds flocking to see your work.


[h1]The not so good[/h1]

Space is a little at a premium, rather like Anno 2205 where, on an entire island, you can maybe build on a quarter of it if that.  I can see why, because a larger park, with the game's micro-management problems, would simply not be doable (more on that below).  Limited space is not itself the biggest issue, however, but that placement of buildings is absolutely infuriating!!   You will find yourself constantly fighting with artificial obstruction and terrain conflict constraints.  You can clear and flatten an area completely, see that the building blueprint visibly fits with space around it, and yet still you will get nonsensical refusals to place your structures.  This is THE most maddening and frustrating part of the game.  It is very difficult to square up buildings to paths, juxtapose buildings in the way the developers did where buildings exist in each park.  I don't think I've encountered placement issues in any game as vexing as this one.

The second major issue is that a smooth-running park, once equipped with a eight or so enclosures, suddenly descends into frenetic micro-management that feels a whole lot more like whack-a-mole than any park management game!  The main issue is not the jobs themselves, but that each action you have to carry out entails lots and lots of clicks through maps, dialogues and menus (there can be a minimum 4-5 menu levels you'll need to cxlick through every time a feeder needs topping up - which is fairly often).  It would be more realistic to allocate enclosures or park zones to keepers than have to do all this yourself manually once you've established your park, but no, park rangers sit dumbly in their buildings until you tell them to look at something.  It interrupts excessively your ability to carry out mission objectives, impedes your ability to keep the park running smoothly and has certainly led me to rage-quit without saving until I've calmed down a bit!

Optional buildings have a questionable service limitation - selling only ONE type of product.  If you open a gift shop, it can ONLY sell stickers, or it can sell an aerosol spray can from the movie, or it can ONLY sell lunch boxes.  If you want to sell all three (and you will need to inorder to have guests contented with shopping, you will have to place three identical buildings.  I imagine this was done to flesh out the 'entertainment' aspect of park design, but it feels a bit artificial, and makes the entertainment aspect more busiwork than it needs to be.

Finally, a lesser issue is the game objectives themselves.  You will often be set a task that's simply not achievable from the island you are on, but you cannot unlock the next island until you've reached a set mission score with the three disciplines of management for the island you're currently working on, leaving you with your mission slots locked with impossible to achieve tasks and seemingly no way to progress.  What the game doesn't tell you is that most of the missions are side missions that you can actually opt out of without penalty, and you will need to do that often.  The most frequent problem mission will be to research a particular species, but the world map hasn't unlocked the research sites for that species, and won't until later in the game from another island.  Some missions are unclear about the parameters (for example: one island will ask you to release a couple of species of dinosaur quite early on in the island's development.  Later, when you have a park full of dinos you are told to cause discomfort to a diplodocus and a velociraptor.  By this stage, you probably have enclosures full of these dinosaurs, but the mission will NOT trigger unless you single out the dinosaurs you released originally at the start of the island level (good luck picking the right ones if you've been merrily incubating entire families)!  

These negatives really put a damper on what is otherwise an excellent game well deserving of its Jurassic Park lineage.  It's a shame.  The game mechanics really feel like they need a bit more thought into ironing out its limitations and frustrations.  These are, after all,  the developers of Planet Coaster, a game which suffers none of these problems and offers much more freedom to be creative in your positioning and layouts.  Questions need to be asked on why a task needs so many clicks and unrealistic micro-management, and why force such tight building placement restrictions on the player when Planet Coaster proves that the developers know how to do it right.


[h1]So, should you buy it?[/h1]

It's a bit pricey.  The base game is worth its price in production value alone, but the additional five dinosaurs behind a 'deluxe' paywall is unfair and unnecessary when the base game is already a premium price.  The extra dinosaurs weren't designed AFTER the game was released so have been paid for with the money of the base game and so people who paid the base price should also get them.  Frontier know people will want ALL the dinosaurs, so it just feels like a cheap and unnecessary stunt to grab more money, which in turn has put more focus on that price than might otherwise have happened.

However, if you want to role-play 'Jurassic Park - The Movie' of your own narrative, this game is perfect for that.  The frustrations really are a problem and might stop you wanting to play it out to the end of the missions, but there is a new sandbox island where you can play without missions and just do your own thing.  I believe that you will get the best out of the game by playing the missions through first, simply because of the scripting and dialogue really needs to be appreciated, but be ready for a few gritted-teeth moments along the way.

[h1] The Game Is Alright, Get It on Sale (TLDR Version at the Bottom of Review)  [/h1]

After 30 hours of gameplay, I’ve found myself doing the same repetitive actions while easily expanding my park in campaign mode. Below, I will try to briefly explain what makes this game easy and repetitive (the core mechanics of the gameplay).

1) Send my dig team out to find fossils. 

2) Extract DNA from the fossils that the dig team found.

3) Once enough DNA is obtained from the fossils, create a dinosaur which results in some profit.

4) While doing steps 1-3, I will sell unused fossils or accept objectives that randomly pop up on my screen which results in easy cash. As a result of the above mechanics, profits are easy to obtain and I eventually find myself with nothing to do besides spamming buildings and dinosaurs everywhere (expanding my park with ease). 

Unfortunately, there is very little to do in terms of micromanagement. Sure, you could set shop prices. Although, because profits are easy to obtain, I never had a reason to do so. Again, profits are rarely an issue. If there is anything that requires some thought in this game, then it would be the placement of said shops, but the game will tell you the best spot for them anyways. I guess, you could say that the game itself does not give you a reason to do much of anything in terms of management. In fact, I never even bothered to research or upgrade certain things unless I realized I needed something specific, such as a specific cure for a sick dinosaur. 

With that said, on a positive note, I will say that modifying your dinosaurs genes (which will raise certain stats, such as its attack or defense) is pretty cool. For example, I put a T-Rex and the Indominus Rex in the same enclosure to watch them fight and to my suprise the T-Rex won because I raised his attack stats by modifying its genes which I did not realize at the time.

Anyways, [b]to add some clarification on steps 1-3, I know it sounds complex or interesting, but it really isn't.[/b] Unfortunately, it's like a mobile game where almost everything has a timer. In other words, you send the dig team out and then you wait a minute or two for them to complete the assignment. After that, you extract DNA from the fossils and wait another minute or two for it to complete. Finally, you create a dinosaur and wait another minute or two for that to complete. I mean, even when you take care of the dinosaurs, you just click on your rangers and tell them to go do a task and wait another minute or two for their tasks to complete. Overall, it's just time consuming and repetitive after the 100th time. I mean, I like the concept but it may not have been executed properly. 

As for the objectives, at least they give you something to do if you choose to. Although, I always end up with a lot of profit so I eventually just ignore all the objectives. Again, the game is pretty easy and it only attempts to challenge you with storms and disasters (i.e. tornadoes that send your velociraptors on a rampage). Plus, these "objectives" are actually known as contracts which are given to you randomly from one of the three divisions in your park. If you favor one of the divisions (meaning you gain a good reputation with them by completing a lot of contracts with them), then the other division will seek to sabatoge your park. Thus, I find it best to ignore most of them unless you are desperate for some cash which usually isn't an issue since profits are easy to obtain. If anything, the only benefit to increasing reputation for these divisions would be unlocking certain buildings and stuff.

Now, if you want an actual challenge, then you could play challenge mode on the hardest difficulty. However, I find that challenge mode is more frustrating (or unfair) rather than challenging. In other words, the game works against you in every way possible and it just kills the enjoyment out of the game. For instance, the goal of challenge mode is to achieve a 5 star rated island as fast as possible. Yet, you start you out with nothing unlocked, meaning that you have to spam dig sites, extract DNA, create dinosaurs, and research everything all over again which is a slow process overall since dinosaurs play a key factor in profits. Remember, these game mechanics all have timers and some of them (such as researching) are extended in challenge mode. Meanwhile, the game throws many obstacles in your path such as The Hammond Foundation taking a large cut of your profits and nature itself trying to nuke you with tornadoes. Overall, challenge mode is just a larger time sink with a higher chance of failure. 

[h1] The Final Verdict (TLDR Version) [/h1]

Long story short, the game is alright if you love Jurassic Park and it’s good in terms of killing time and just having [b]casual[/b] fun. However, you will most likely get bored or upset if you buy this game expecting a lot of depth or difficulty when it comes to building and park management stuff. If you’re looking for depth or a fair challenge, then you might want to look elsewhere. Aside from the lack of difficutly, the core mechanics of the game can be frustrating at times. With all of that said, the game is beautiful, the music is chill, and performance isn’t an issue. I definitely recommend the game on sale for some casual fun. Did you ever play Rollercoaster Tycoon? or any of its successors and rip offs?  Well, let me be very clear that this game is absolutely nothing like those games.  Those games were much, much more fun yet way less awesome in scope and possibility as this game.  Oh, the possibility of this game and what it could have been and could still be.

Remember placing down drink stalls in those games, some crap attractions like a ferris wheel and small rides that were basically a 4x4 building?  This game has that!  In bulk!  Remember the fun of designing and building a roller coaster that had a rating based on its design that would make some visitors happy and some wouldn't want to go on it?  Yeah, that is not present.  Instead you get to design and build a dinosaur enclosure that has nothing at all to do with attendance or someones interest in visiting it.

Why do people come here?  To see the dinosaurs.  I guess its like a dinosaur zoo.  And I don't mean like Bush Gardens in Florida that has attractions like rides and coasters.... no, no, no.  This is like building a technological version of your local zoo.

The game looks great though!  It is very polished.  It just lacks everything fun that made this entire genre.

Your designed enclosures, just make sure your dinosaurs don't get cranky and try to escape.  Put down a fence, add some trees and a pond, bam, create a few dinosaurs and move on to the next one.  The enclosure doesnt make your park any more or less attractive to visitors, the type of dinosaur you create does.  

How do you create better dinosaurs?  You send your teams out on a mission that collects fossils and then extract dna from those fossils and add traits to the dinosaurs.  This is a repetative and boring task where you click a button, wait, click another button, wait, click another button and wait.  I don't think people would consider this "fun".  This is the majority of your game time.

Yes, the majority of your game time is spent waiting for cash (that is based on a cash per minute cycle based on your overall park prestige rating which is based on the prestige levels of the dinosaurs inside your park), sending out your teams to dig, waiting for them to dig, sending the fossils over to extract new DNA, waiting for the DNA to extract, then repeat.  Finally after awhile you will be able to create new modified dinosaurs to up your cash per minute!  That's the entire game.

I guess you can do other stuff, more of like a one off or a 20 minute divergence from the main objectives of the game, like, let your dinosaurs escape on purpose and eat visitors.  Or you could drive around in your jeep (or helicopter) and snap photos.... ugh N64 pokemon snap anyone?  You could shoot your dinosaurs with tranq darts, or put different types of carnivor dinosaurs together and let them fight it out.  These things may seem like really nice extras, but they are boring and for the most part not really worth doing after having done them a few times.

So now that you've made your park and finished the first island, lets go to the next island and make a new park there.  I guess the last guy sucked at placing a few buildings and waiting for DNA... so since you're much better at waiting, its up to you to fix it!  The best way to beat the other levels is.... destroy everything on them and start over from scratch.  Kind of like building the first park 5 different times on 5 different islands!  Oh joy!

Of course along the way, new fossil sites open up, new dinosaur types open, and that is nice.  You will have more stuff to look at while you wait.  Making a dinosaur can be satisfying the first time, the camera pans in and you can watch it get released into the enclosure.... and then when you realize you have to do that EVERY time you make a new one... it becomes a chore and is just obnoxious.

Now the biggest and most glaring issue is the path's.  What is the purpose of a path you might ask.  Well in a normal game, people would use it to get to attractions they want to visit.  You could click on those visitors to see what they like and dislike and what they want and need..... im sorry, the people are just there to add "life" to the scene, you cannot interact with guests.  In this game the paths just seem super arbitrary and is only required in order to place a building and serve no other purpose at present.

Admitedly, I did play through all of the parks, not because it was fun per say, but because I literally didn't have anything better to do.  It is very satisfying to build up a super amazingly designed park and then look at it as you fly around in your helicopter... but you'd better have a book to read on the side while getting to that point, because you will be bored.

I guess some people really like the game because "dinosaurs", but just like they said in the movies, "dinosaurs" just aren't enough anymore, you have to up the ante.  And this game needs to up the ante by.... like.... a lot.

Again, wish there was a 'meh' rating.  So, here's where it is at after the last patch (only played since).  I think the game has potential... some day... but dear lord don't pay $60 for this. CON: 
* even after patch no real 'pack' feel for anything - fights are always 1:1 and feel that way, 

* the different 'branches' giving you missions are meaningless aside from the voice (security asks you to research genomes, science asks you to make money, etc)

'look jim, that's a pretty sky' 'yes martha, that is a pretty sky'.  When dinos run through them you don't even feel all that satisfied watching them die because, except for a few giant carnis..:

It didn't even notice them.  

* dinos are wrong.  They are true to the movie so that's ok, but they're still wrong versus what the dinos should actually be in real life.  So don't go bothering to read the descriptions thinking you're learning something, you're not, you're learning movie lore and not dino lore

* dinos get boring.  Sad as that may be, once you've unlocked a few... they don't... 'do' anything.  The carnis have some personality and you get them fighting because you're just bored and need some drama, otherwise they just... I mean, I don't know what I'd expect them to do I guess?   But they don't do it.  They do look pretty though so that's cool.  But I don't know, just different skins over animations means I don't particularly care about unlocking more dinos.  I wish the herbivores showed a bit more personality - individually, or as species.  And maybe it is there, hidden in the AI's decision of when to roam vs run vs eat vs drink.  But it doesn't come across.  Have the smaller dinos play with each other.  Have the bigger ones circle up to defend from predators, or chase off smaller ones from food when they're eating.  Have the headbutting ones head-butt each other for dominance.  Have more talking bits when you select dinos so you learn neat things about them, or some offshoot of 'crikey, this dino is bad tempered and dangerous.  I'm gonna poke it with a stick'.  Just.... something to do or watch or listen to during the long long periods of just sitting there waiting on money or unlocks

* 'hours'.  I guess this is the most missleading term in gaming.  At this moment Steam tells me I have played '26 hours'.  Wow, I got my money's worth!  But... did I?  I have had this game running for 26 hours.  How much have I actually 'played'?  How much have I spent making interesting decisions I was excited about?  Seeing neat things?  Mmm... a fraction of that.  Not 0, there are fun parts to this game.... But not 26 by any means.  

CONCLUSION:  This isn't a terrible game.  It is a time-waster with pretty graphics.  When you put it down you don't feel you've accomplished much you're proud of.  But it is fine to play in the background while watching youtube or doing something else, so... not terrible.  And you can see the seed of something potentially great in there, if it doesn't get stuck on trying to crank out money-making DLC before fixing the core game and making THAT playable and fun.  So... if it is on sale for $20, and you have $20 to throw away, there are worse place to toss it.  Otherwise maybe wait for a few more patches until you hear that these things have gotten fixed in the core game.  And don't worry about any DLC released until then - a few extra skins (oh look!  there's an even prettier dino that does nothing!  and that is totally fictional so you can't even say you're buying it because you just love dinosours) won't fix the parts of this game you won't enjoy.

The gameplay is very limited in comparision to Operation Genesis. It might be a fun game for some people but for me there are these gamebreaking design choices that do not make it worth 55-60€:
- No fresh start Freeplay Parkbuilding. Only Campaign where you unlock stuff for the unlimited money small island creative sandbox
- Sandbox is locked behind a 4 star rating on your first island
-"Dinosaurs will remain tranquilised until airlifted, so this seems to be working as intended." QA Team on Frontier Forum
- Guests behave very simply. 
- No interaction between player and guests
- Vehicles can not be destroyed
- Dinos behave very scripted and are for example ignoring guests inside the enclosure because they didnot trigger the event (had 2 guests trapped inside a ceratosaurus cage and it ignored them for over 1h ingame time)
- No way to rescue guests from danger 
- No day/night cycle only fixed lightning depending on the island
- no building/shop customisation beside paint and name
- no decorations like parkbenches, statues, flowerbeds etc.
- limited set of animations (1 per acion)
- very limited building spaces
- mouse controlls on pc are based on console controlls
- only 1 hybrid possible
- dinos do not need to sleep
- only 5 island no random map with a mission for each department so 15 missions total
- limited interaction with dinos compared to operation genesis(only tranq,move,cure and photo)
- no workshop or modsupport for now (and maybe not in the future thanks to universal studios)

Shelfing this until this "coming soon" patch comes out. Started the game being amazed at the dinosaurs but that wears off pretty quickly unfortunetly. By the end of the 3rd island I had to stop. The tedium and lack of customization is just too glaring for me to continue at the moment. I recently started playing operation genesis again and while the graphics haven't aged that well, the mechanics in that game are for the most part superior to those of this game. You actually have to tend to the park-goer's needs making sure they're enjoying the dinosaurs/attractions and if they leave unsatisfied, try to rectify that by improving your park. There's also automation in genesis such as the feeders/dig teams that make it a much smoother experience. I'm sure this game will eventually get there, but if I know anything about Frontier's games from playing Elite, it's that they take forever to patch their games. It might be a worthy successor to JPOG in two years from now when the 3rd patch comes out (heh), but hold off on it at least until it goes on sale. Nostalgia sure is a bitch.

Basically, a very expensive mobile phone level kinda game. Very overpriced for what it's offering and feels like a simple cash cow that is using a famous brand tag for it. Despite the pretty looks, it fails to truly match or beat it's spiritual predecessor Jurassic Park Operation Genesis. The expensive DLCs, lack of good quality iconic movie skins, lack of freeform map generator and lack of many other key components that make games like this appealing is an insult to my intelligence as a fan of the franchise and somebody who values a good quality product. Put the price down all the way to 50% on literally everything and perhaps we can have that conversation again. But I personally feel cheated for what I was charged and will be reluctant to give the devs my money again.

[b]Jurassic World Evolution[/b] is the best movie tie-in game I've played in years, the best park management game I've played in years, and maybe the best dinosaur game I've ever played in my life. If you're a fan of any of these three things, check this game out; if you're a fan of all three, this game is a [i]no-brainer[/i], and I guarantee you'll enjoy it more than you think. There's a lot of love and attention to detail in this one, more than it may seem at first glance.

Obviously what needs to be said about [b]Jurassic World Evolution[/b] is that it absolutely nails its most important feature - the dinosaurs. They are [i]film[/i] accurate dinosaurs (no feathered animals here), their design is just fantastic, and the game provides countless opportunities for you to just LOOK at them, to be among them, to be mesmerized by their dinosaur-ness, their unique ways of moving, eating, socializing, roaring... and fighting. The dinosaurs in this game look and sound amazing, and they elevate the park management experience to another level entirely. Practically every single species you can create is dangerous in some way, and the game makes you constantly aware of this. You must respect these animals and their needs or they will absolutely run amok, and that's the way it should be. Believe me, you won't forget what it feels like when your first dinosaur escapes.

As a park management game, there are certainly ways in ways in which [b]Jurassic World Evolution[/b] could be better. There aren't a ton of options where non-dinosaur attractions and amenities are concerned (DLC's add some cool stuff though), but again, that's not really what the game is going for. This game is an excuse to geek out about dinosaurs, to feel their presence, to feel scared and exhilarated by them, to feel childlike wonder, to feel [i]emotions[/i]. It is in this way that [b]Jurassic World Evolution[/b] deserves praise, it creates legitimately emotional moments and sequences. Sometimes that emotion comes from seeing mixed herds of dinosaurs slowly walking among trees, vocalizing among themselves as the sun sets in the distance, sometimes it comes from manually driving a slipping and sliding Jeep to go fix a broken fence in the middle of a crazy tropical storm, and sometimes it comes from hearing a [i]Tyrannosaurus[/i] roar echoing across your park as you deal with mundane management issues. This game transports you to your own Jurassic Park and reminds you of how awesome dinosaurs are, and that's all I could ask from it.

The reviews for this game are unnecessarily harsh. This is a fantastic management simulator, and a really great dinosaur game. I have played without any of the DLCs, and there are dozens of dinosaur species, lots of buildings types, maybe 50 research items, and some definite challenges. I've beaten the campaign, and I do recommend the game and I would pay full price for it again.

Other reviews I have read call the game shallow due to formulaic dinosaur interactions, but it isn't. Dinosaurs have comfort levels, and if they are too low, the dinosaurs will attack each other and the enclosures. The factors that cause each dinosaur are different. Some dinosaurs, especially large carnivores, don't want competition from their own species. The herbivores all want company, and some of them are happy with many different species, which results in dinosaur enclosures with 10 different species of dinosaurs living in harmony. All the dinosaurs have different requirements in terms of space and biomes, simplified down to the area of forest, plain, and water they require. A brontosaurus requires a massive enclosure, while the small guys are okay with something akin to a zoo enclosure.

To complicate things, the dinosaurs can be genetically modified which can change their base stats, but also make them more (or less) social, more violent, more or less disease resistant, even increase their lifespan. To further complicate things, dinosaurs start to lose comfort in randomly  occuring tropical storms, and the dangerous predators (think velociraptors, tyrannosaurus rex, and especially the genetic hybrids from the two Jurassic World films- the indominus rex and the indoraptor) have super high thresholds for comfort before they attack their enclosure and murder your guests.

The other complain I've seen is a lack of space constraining the player's creativity. This is the big challenge on the campaign maps, of which there are 5. They have crazy shapes, some are very small, all are designed to give environmental challenges and force the player to have different dinosaur species interacting to meet the mission goals. If you had an infinite canvas, players would put each dinosaur type in its own pen and the game would be easy but boring. Instead, through trial and error, the player discovers that velociraptors play well with armored herbivores like the ankylosaurus, but they will eat parasaurs, and carnotaurus eats them. I appreciate that after the fourth campaign map, which is a long, thin island, my knowledge of dinosaur interaction increased the the point where I knew MUCH more about dinosaur interactions in the game than before. Take that to the sandbox mode (which there is one, Isla Nublar), and you will be able to pack more dinosaurs into smaller areas for more money and guest enjoyment. The campaign maps train the player.

Definitely play this game if you like management simulators. This game is the best zoo management game I've played, and also a great dinosaur-themed game. Highly recommended.
